USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the March 1 clock running and negotiate hard in the current high-level round without new tariff hikes, new entity-list moves, or any rollback. Take Chinese purchase offers as a down payment, not a deal. Insist that any path off the List 3 10-to-25 percent hike include enforceable commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, and verification—the issues that collapsed the May 2018 truce. Keep the Huawei/Meng criminal process on a separate legal track and do not trade it for a purchase package.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly above neutral, not high and not an opportunity. The US already covers ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%) and China is at the table, which is leverage. But the original Section 301 complaint is still unmet: the 2019-01-07 and 2019-01-30 rounds discussed purchases while structural IP/tech-transfer and enforcement remained open, and Lighthizer told Ways and Means in mid-January he would not extend the March 1 deadline. That cliff is useful only if it is not fired blindly. Offset: China’s retaliation has already hit a core US export constituency—soy sales to China fell ~94% through mid-October, September US-to-China bean shipments were down >80%, and USDA/ASA documented a ~$2/bushel price break plus $12B in stopgap farm aid. US consumer sentiment dropped from 100.1 to 91.2 and industrial production slipped into January; the 10-year yield fell to 2.70% and the curve flattened, showing markets are pricing slower growth even as VIX cooled from the December 36 spike to 17.66. The 2019-01-28 Huawei/Meng indictments and extradition request, unsealed as Liu He arrived, add a second front Beijing calls political suppression; treating that as a trade chip would either blow up talks or sell out a sanctions/IP case. Escalating tariffs now would likely trigger matching Chinese retaliation and deepen farm and market stress with ~30 days still on the clock. Conceding purchases or a partial rollback would repeat May 19–29 (Mnuchin “on hold,” then the White House reopened 301). Negotiate, hold existing tariffs, and make March 2 the priced alternative if structure and enforcement are not on paper.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the 90-day G20 window open and treat the 30–31 January Lighthizer–Mnuchin talks as a chance to lock in a purchases-heavy interim package that can stop the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25% on 1 March. Offer large, front-loaded, verifiable buys of US soy, energy and manufactures as the bargaining chip Trump can sell at home, and discuss enforceable IP/cyber process improvements—but do not concede core industrial-policy or Made in China 2025 architecture, and do not add new tariffs or widen the Kovrig/Spavor track. Separate the Meng/Huawei legal fight from the tariff negotiation so a criminal case cannot blow up a truce we need for growth and jobs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 September 2018), and the G20 truce only suspended—did not cancel—the 1 January hike of List 3 to 25%, now hanging over 1–2 March. That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor: major export sectors are hit, Huawei is being firm-targeted, and export-hub employment risk is rising. The real-economy bite is visible: China’s 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% (Q4 6.4%), the weakest in about three decades; December exports fell 4.4% and imports 7.6%; eight provinces cut 2019 growth targets; US goods imports from China dropped ~17% from September to January (IMPCH $49.9B to $41.3B). The 16 April 2018 ZTE denial order plus the 1 December Meng arrest, 10 December Canadian detentions, and 28 January DOJ Huawei/Meng indictment show a second, more dangerous track: US component leverage over national tech champions. That is why the score sits slightly above +0.5 rather than at 0—the tariff clock and the entity-list/extradition track are now running together. It is not +0.8/+1.0 because the truce is still in force, high-level talks are underway, Trump is market-sensitive after the December vol spike (VIX peaked at 36.07 on 24 December), and stimulus tools remain. Action should not match threat with escalation: a new Chinese tariff wave or wider hostage diplomacy would likely collapse the window, trigger the March hike, and risk the remaining ~$267B list. May 2018 already showed a purchases-only “trade war on hold” can be reversed by hawks; Lighthizer is in the room precisely to block an empty soybean deal and is telling Congress the March deadline will not be extended. So the right stance is negotiate (action ~+0.1): use purchases and limited IP process concessions to buy a freeze or delay, hold the line on structural control of the industrial model, and avoid both unilateral rollback and further retaliation until Washington puts matching tariff relief on the table.
